topFindings.description: 6 cases assert task structure on a helper run.ts:59-64 marks '@deprecated WM-1 ... No production caller remains'; duplicated at run-overhaul.test.ts:25-30 and multi-provider-spawn-kill-run.test.ts:180-182, masking the absence of coverage on the buildExecutionRequest+resolveToTask replacement.

metaRootCause.verdict:
Deckent does not keep breaking basic features in spite of its scale and instrumentation — it breaks them BECAUSE of how that scale and instrumentation were built. The system has a vast, sophisticated control plane (RBAC authority matrix, proof-of-function gates, honest-gate downgrades, cross-verify, post-sprint smoke, panic guards, capability least-privilege, tenant isolation, prompt-evolution feedback, telemetry, notification dispatch) that is overwhelmingly DECLARED but not ENFORCED. Across every layer the same five mechanisms repeat: (1) gates default to advisory/soft and return success regardless of verdict (worker authority `checkWorkerAuthority` returns true in both branches; `enforceRbac` is a NO_OP when `enabled` is false and the default IS false; PanicGuard BLOCK is ignored; mTLS cert detected-then-ignored; spawn-safety never enforced); (2) the verification spine is unwired or stubbed (proof-of-function gate, post-sprint smoke runner is a `passed:true` no-op stub, `runHonestyCheck` literally `return 0`, applyTechDebtDowngrade, cross-verify REFUTED — all dead or trusting worker self-report); (3) config knobs proliferate that are validated and displayed but never read (rollback_policy, strictTenantIsolation, telemetry_*, cost caps, boundary_enforcement, adaptive-timeout, native skills) — settings that lie to the operator; (4) silent fallback / override-drop everywhere (provider health read into empty if-body, notification config accepted but never delivered, fail-safe catch-and-continue hooks that swallow errors, getMessage returns the key on miss); (5) metrics that feed the learning/decay/eval loops are hardcoded zero (boundaryViolations=0, coverage=0, prompt version stats {uses:0}, debt-rate 0%, history scaling factor permanently 1.0), so the self-improvement and self-audit loops the project relies on to "catch drift" are structurally inert. The result is a closed circle: the safeguards that would detect a broken feature are themselves the broken features, and because they fail OPEN and SILENT, every sprint can be marked green while real regressions ship.

The deeper structural enabler is that deckent has no single source of truth and no hard architectural boundary. The same concept is reimplemented 3-5 times with divergent semantics (three RateLimiters, three parseVitestOutput, three getCurrentSprintId reading different files, two ROLE_CAPABILITY_MAPs, two NervousSystemConfig schemas, two evaluateResult, two notification systems, duplicate checkWorkerAuthority, noGoRate as both percentage and fraction in live paths), so a fix applied to one copy silently leaves the live copy untouched — this is precisely why "advertised fixes" (skill-affinity routing, agent imbalance, tenant IDOR filter) are no-ops: the fix landed in a module nobody calls. ESM import discipline is soft (bare require() in pure-ESM modules falls back silently; ADR-087 async mandate violated by spawnSync in hot paths across a dozen files), and "DONE" is accepted on trust rather than disk-verified, so false-DONE acceptance is the default acceptance. To actually hold a chain of success, deckent must flip its enforcement philosophy: gates must fail CLOSED by default with the block path reachable in standard config, the verification spine (smoke/proof-of-function/honesty/disk-verify) must be wired into the finalize path and run against real binary output, every config knob must have a runtime reader asserted by a "no dormant knob" lint, duplicates must be collapsed to one canonical implementation, and the metrics that drive eval/learning must be populated from real data — otherwise adding more tooling only adds more places for drift to hide.

rootCauses.title: Enforcement is structurally advisory: every security/quality gate fails OPEN by default and the hard-block path is unreachable in standard config
rootCauses.mechanism: The system's gates are written to warn-and-permit rather than deny. checkWorkerAuthority returns true in BOTH the violation and non-violation branches (worker.ts:602-620), so scope enforcement is a literal no-op. enforceRbac is a NO_OP whenever rbacConfig.enabled is false (rbac.ts:127) and the config default is enabled:false (config.ts:1192) with no mechanism to flip it, so the entire RBAC authority matrix is permanently advisory across worker, nervous, sprint-runtime, backlog-trigger, and autonomous paths. PanicGuard BLOCK is ignored (worker kill proceeds anyway), mTLS cert presence is detected/warned/then ignored, assertSpawnSafe (ADR-006) is never called at spawn callsites, and DockerSpawnBackend (the DEFAULT backend) bypasses the SAFETY_FLOOR lethal guard entirely. Because the deny path is never reached, a violating worker, an over-privileged action, or a lethal command is silently permitted — and the audit trail that would record it is itself often soft (canAutoApply veto logged only to console.log, not audit history). This lets every boundary breach survive to ship while the dashboard stays green.
rootCauses.fixDirection: Invert the default: gates fail CLOSED. Wire enforce_rbac with a real config default of true and a validated schema field (not a type-cast); make checkWorkerAuthority actually return result.allowed; route every spawn callsite through assertSpawnSafe; make PanicGuard/mTLS BLOCK terminate execution. Add a 'no advisory-only gate' lint that fails CI if a function named enforce*/check*/assert* has a code path that returns success on a deny verdict.

rootCauses.title: The verification spine is unwired or stubbed — DONE is accepted on worker self-report, not disk-verified (trust-without-verify)
rootCauses.mechanism: Every mechanism designed to independently CONFIRM a worker actually did the work is either dead code or a no-op stub. runPostSprintSmoke/applyProofOfFunctionGate/verifyProofOfFunction have zero production callers (imported but never called in sprint-reporter.ts:97), and even if wired the defaultSmokeRunner unconditionally returns passed:true with output 'default smoke runner (no-op stub)' (post-sprint-smoke.ts:227-232). runHonestyCheck is a literal `return 0` stub (sprint-finalizer.ts:156), so the honesty gate in runSelfAuditGate can never trigger. applyTechDebtDowngrade and checkVerifyMarkerHonesty have zero callers; the verify-delta gate accepts the worker's DONE claim without ever reading the verify-delta file it mandates. reconcileRubricNoGo flips Brain NO_GO to DONE using worker-self-reported coverage as ground truth, and cross-verify REFUTED verdicts are purely advisory with no enforcement path. SubprocessSpawnBackend awards GO_WITH_TECH_DEBT to exit-0 workers that never wrote a result file. The net effect: a worker (or an LLM hallucinating success) can claim DONE and the orchestrator has no independent ground-truth check standing between that claim and a green sprint — exactly the false-DONE acceptance that lets broken features ship sprint after sprint.
rootCauses.fixDirection: Wire the verification spine into the finalize path and make it real: replace defaultSmokeRunner's no-op with an actual real-binary run against the task's declared Smoke command; implement runHonestyCheck against disk diff; make Brain disk-verify (git diff --stat / ls-files) the result before accepting DONE rather than trusting worker self-report or worker-reported coverage. Treat 'verify task exists but ran a stub' as NO_GO. Add a test that fails if any *Gate/*Smoke/*Honesty export has zero production callers.

rootCauses.title: Dormant-knob proliferation — config fields that are defined, validated, displayed, and documented but never read at runtime (settings that lie)
rootCauses.mechanism: A large fraction of the configuration surface has no runtime reader, so operators (and the dashboard ConfigPage) believe they are controlling behavior that is hardcoded. rollback_policy is validated and documented but its value is never read (rollback is hardcoded to opts.rollback!==false); strictTenantIsolation defaults false and is never threaded to MemoryStore (guaranteeing tenant data leak); enforce_least_privilege and denialAudit never reach createAuditedCapabilityRegistry; daily_max_usd/monthly_max_usd are settable and displayed but never enforced as a spending gate; boundary_enforcement, cost_optimization, telemetry_enabled/anonymous, output_render_mode, sandboxMode, adaptive-timeout knobs, history_scaling_enabled, mcp_client_enabled, native_cost_ceiling_usd, plugin_require_signature, --auto-approve (hardcoded true), --tenant, --local — all defined-but-inert. Some are read via unsafe type-casts that bypass schema validation entirely (autonomous.engine='v2', risk_gate_enabled, native_cost_ceiling). This destroys the operator's mental model: turning a safety/cost/tenant knob ON changes nothing, so a misconfiguration that should be caught is silently ignored, and 'I enabled the gate' is false.
rootCauses.fixDirection: Establish a 'no dormant knob' invariant: every field in the config schema must have at least one production read-site asserted by a registry test (the test enumerates schema keys and greps for a runtime reader, failing CI on any orphan). Remove fields marked 'legacy — never wired' from the default config. Ban reading config via type-cast — any field a code path reads must be declared on DeckentConfig and validated.

rootCauses.title: No single source of truth — the same concept is reimplemented 3-5 times with divergent semantics, so fixes land in dead copies while the live path is untouched
rootCauses.mechanism: Core abstractions exist in multiple incompatible copies with no shared canonical implementation, and routing/dispatch frequently selects a different copy than the one a fix was applied to. There are three divergent RateLimiter implementations, three parseVitestOutput, three getCurrentSprintId reading three different files, three extractKeywords, three redactSensitive with different regex coverage, three max_workers algorithms, two ROLE_CAPABILITY_MAP definitions (with conflicting roles), two NervousSystemConfig schemas (one field required in one and optional in the other), two evaluateResult with different logic, two waitForResults (the DI one never called), two notification systems, duplicate checkWorkerAuthority with divergent signatures, and noGoRate stored as percent in one live path and consumed as fraction in another. This is precisely why advertised fixes are no-ops: the skill-affinity routing fix lives in activation-engine code the routing engine's selectBestAgent skips; the lineage tenant IDOR filter exists but server.ts dispatches the route without `req` so the filter is bypassed; enforceRbac in core/rbac.ts is never imported because enforcement reimplements it inline. Every divergent copy is a place where a regression can hide behind a passing test of its twin.
rootCauses.fixDirection: Collapse each duplicated concept to one canonical module and delete the rest (RateLimiter, parseVitestOutput, getCurrentSprintId, ROLE_CAPABILITY_MAP, NervousSystemConfig, redactSensitive, max_workers). Add a duplicate-export lint that flags two exported symbols with the same name/role across modules. For routing/dispatch fixes, require a live-path integration test that exercises the actual production call chain (not the helper in isolation) so a fix in a dead copy fails the test.

rootCauses.title: Feedback/learning/audit loops run on hardcoded-zero metrics — the self-improvement machinery is structurally inert and cannot detect its own drift
rootCauses.mechanism: Deckent's claimed differentiators (self-learning routing, prompt evolution, debt decay, boundary-violation tracking, honesty calibration, telemetry) all depend on metrics that are never populated, so the loops execute but learn nothing. SprintMetrics.boundaryViolations is always hardcoded 0 (so the retro boundary check is permanently wrong), coverage is always 0 throughout the CI guardian and process-runtime makeProcessResult (linesAdded/Removed/coverage all 0), PromptVersion.stats is frozen at {uses:0,successRate:0} because updateVersionStats is never called (F5 evolution loop is permanently silent), DebtTrendAnalyzer always computes 0% debt rate (detector permanently inert), history_scaling_enabled is true by default but SprintHistory is always zero-filled making historyFactor permanently 1.0, recordCrossVerifyVerdict is never called so REFUTED signals never feed routing, and assessSkillRelevance/LearningConfig fields never reach OutcomeTracker. Because the metrics that would surface 'this feature regressed' or 'this agent is failing' are constant zeros, the system has no closed feedback loop to catch breakage — it is instrumented but blind, which is why scale and tooling have not translated into a held chain of success.
rootCauses.fixDirection: Populate the metrics from real data at their source: boundaryViolations from the auditor's git-diff scan, coverage from parsed vitest JSON, prompt stats from retro outcomes, debt rate from the debt store. Add assertions that a metric feeding a learning/decay loop is non-constant across sprints (a test that flags any metric hardcoded to 0/literal). Wire recordCrossVerifyVerdict and version-stats updates into the retro phase so the feedback loop actually closes.

rootCauses.title: Silent fallback / swallowed-error / unwired-feature is the default failure mode — features fail invisibly instead of surfacing
rootCauses.mechanism: When a path cannot complete its job, the pervasive pattern is to swallow the error and report success rather than fail loudly. bootstrapProviders reads the health-check result into an empty if-body (unhealthy providers have no effect); detectClaude reports authMethod='session' unconditionally with no real login check; config-driven Slack/Discord/Webhook notifications are accepted but the old dispatcher is superseded-not-removed so messages are silently never sent (notify-bootstrap trust-without-verify gap); the dashboard session token is never forwarded to API fetches so authenticated requests silently return nothing and the 401 event has no listener; kill/cleanup errors are swallowed in SprintControlPanel and WorkersPage with no user feedback; runPostFinalizeHooks and runAllUpdaters catch-and-continue with no way to surface failures; getMessage returns the key string on a missing key so i18n typos are invisible; Discord sendMessage drops messages for unknown channels; nextSequence claims atomic but is a racy read-modify-write. On top of this, a huge swath of built features are simply never wired (entire CLI helper review subsystem of 8 classes, dashboard analytics classes, SandboxSpawnBackend, BedrockAdapter spawn always throws, deckent_kill only marks PAUSED without killing the process, deckent_plan documented dry-run but writes files, chat --native wires a stub dispatcher returning placeholders). A feature that fails silently or was never connected looks identical to a working one until a user hits it — which is the literal definition of shipping broken basics.
rootCauses.fixDirection: Make silent failure illegal on user-facing and security paths: surface caught errors to the sprint outcome / UI instead of catch-and-continue; have getMessage throw (or log+flag) on missing keys in dev; forward the session token in the shared fetch layer and add a 401 listener. Adopt a 'no orphan export' rule — any exported production symbol with zero callers must be either wired or deleted, enforced by a periodic dead-code audit, so 'built but never connected' cannot accumulate.

rootCauses.title: Soft architectural rules (ESM discipline, async I/O standard, scope sanitizer) are documented but not mechanically enforced, allowing slow erosion
rootCauses.mechanism: ADRs that are supposed to be load-bearing constraints are honored by convention only, so violations accumulate silently. ADR-087 (async I/O, no spawnSync) is violated by spawnSync in at least a dozen hot/async paths — planner, mid-sprint-adapter, baseline-tracker captureVitestBaseline, task-restoration inside async finalizeSprint, monitor-adapter, output-collector polling loop, onboard, realPlannerComplete in the JIT hot path — each capable of freezing the event loop and causing the timeouts that masquerade as worker failures. ADR-001/002 (pure ESM) is violated by bare require('fs') in promotion-pipeline and require() in nervous runtime-scope-check, which 'always silently falls back to stderr' (the scope-violation event is never emitted). The scope-sanitizer JSDoc claims 8 rules but the code runs 10 with ordering gaps and fails to protect prefixed protected files (src/package.json). Because nothing fails the build when an ADR is violated, the codebase erodes one 'small' exception at a time, and the very ADR-governance the project markets as its rigor is not wired to block anything.
rootCauses.fixDirection: Turn ADR constraints into mechanical lint gates: ban spawnSync in async modules via an ESLint/tsc rule (allowlist only documented sync-startup paths), ban bare require() in the ESM package, and reconcile scope-sanitizer rules with its doc + add prefix-aware protected-file matching. Wire enforceAdrCompliance (currently zero production callers and fails-open on error) into the actual evaluation path so an ADR violation is a real NO_GO rather than a doc.

rootCauses.title: Test theater — mock-only suites and tests pinned to dead code report green while the live path is unverified
rootCauses.mechanism: A meaningful slice of the test suite asserts on mocks, stubs, or already-dead production code, producing green CI that proves nothing about real behavior — the inverse of the project's own proof-of-function mandate. notification-flow.test.ts tests the dead old NotificationDispatcher, not the live pipeline; cross-sprint-analyzer.test.ts and the vscode extension.test.ts test dead/stub classes; agentic-session.test.ts mocks the entire MemoryStore so it verifies mock behavior, not DB persistence; formatDoctorResponse tests use synthetic {ok:} data that never matches real checks (and the real formatter reports all checks failed due to an .ok vs .passed mismatch); SprintControlPanel.test.tsx encodes the component's silent-error behavior as expected for an unwired component; dashboard nav/i18n tests check only a subset of routes/pages and miss the ones with confirmed hardcoded strings; worker-grid-live.test.tsx asserts on source-text strings instead of component behavior. Because these suites are green, they actively mask the underlying breakage and give false confidence that the chain of success is holding.
rootCauses.fixDirection: Require behavior-level assertions on the live path: forbid tests that import a symbol with zero production callers (a test referencing dead code should fail a meta-test); replace whole-store mocks with tmpdir-backed real DBs for persistence tests; assert on real served HTML / real CLI stdout per the proof-of-function DoD; expand nav/i18n coverage tests to enumerate ALL routes/pages rather than a hardcoded subset so new surfaces cannot slip through unverified.

confirmed.title: checkWorkerAuthority in agents/worker.ts returns true in BOTH branches — authority check is a structural no-op
confirmed.evidence: Lines 602–620: `if (!result.allowed) { console.warn(...); ... return true; } return true;` — both the violation branch and the permit branch return `true`, so the function can never signal a scope violation to its caller, regardless of the ADR-037 decision.
confirmed.description: The exported `checkWorkerAuthority` function in `src/agents/worker.ts` (line 584) wraps `authority-enforcer.checkAuthority` but unconditionally returns `true` in every code path. The `!result.allowed` branch logs a warning and emits an event, then returns `true` (line 617) instead of `false`. The non-violation branch also returns `true` (line 620). Any caller relying on a `false` return to block a write would never receive it. Line 374 only returns `allowed: false` when `enforceRbac === true`. autonomous/runtime-loop.ts lines 281-282: `const spawn = checkSprintSpawnRbac(req, config, audit); if (!spawn.allowed) return { allowed: false, ... }` — the gate is wired but `allowed` is always `true` in default deployments.

The architecture acknowledges this: the code comment says 'ADR-037 V1.0 soft-warn' and 'hard-flip post-GA V2', but there is no mechanism that escalates from warn to block. The structural root cause is that the opt-in flag defaults to `false` with no enforcement deadline, meaning operator inaction perpetuates the open gate indefinitely.

confirmed.title: audit-writer.ts chainHead is a process-wide singleton — cross-sprint chain verification always fails brokenAt:0

In a long-lived process (MCP server, API server, autonomous runtime-loop with `auditSprintId = getCurrentSprintId() ?? 'autonomous'`), Sprint-B's first event has `prevHmac` pointing to Sprint-A's last hash; `verifyAuditChain(sprint-B-events)` returns `{ intact: false, brokenAt: 0 }` immediately because `sprint-B[0].prevHmac != GENESIS_HMAC`.

In short-lived CLI invocations (one sprint per process) this is harmless; in long-running processes such as the autonomous runtime-loop, MCP server, or HTTP API server, every sprint after the first will have its first event's `prevHmac` point to the previous sprint's last hash — not to GENESIS. Calling `verifyAuditChain` on any such sprint's events in isolation will immediately return `{ intact: false, brokenAt: 0 }`, producing persistent false-positive integrity failures that mask real tampering.

confirmed.title: audit-writer.ts uses unkeyed SHA-256 but names the field 'hmac'; audit-export.ts uses keyed HMAC-SHA256 — incompatible chains
confirmed.evidence: audit-writer.ts line 166-169: `function computeEventHmac(prevHmac: string, basePayload: unknown): string { const h = createHash('sha256'); h.update(prevHmac + canonicalJson(basePayload)); return h.digest('hex'); }` — uses `createHash` (unkeyed). The field storing this is `AuditEvent.hmac` (line 44: 'sha256(prevHmac + canonicalJson(payload_without_chain_fields))'). audit-export.ts line 113-116: `const digest = createHmac('sha256', secret).update(prev + JSON.stringify(entry)).join(',') — uses `createHmac` with `secret` (default 'deckent-audit'). The two 'chains' are computed differently and on different input structures (canonical JSON vs standard JSON.stringify), making them mutually unverifiable.
confirmed.description: The in-stream chain built by `writeAuditEvent` uses an unkeyed SHA-256 hash (`createHash`), while the export chain built by `exportAuditLog` uses a keyed HMAC-SHA256 (`createHmac`). Additionally, the internal chain uses `canonicalJson` (sorted-key deterministic serialization) over the full `AuditEventPayload`, while the export chain uses `JSON.stringify(entry)` with key ordering determined by insertion order. The `verifyHmacChain` function in audit-export.ts cannot verify the in-stream chain, and `verifyAuditChain` in audit-writer.ts cannot verify the export chain. The field is misleadingly named 'hmac' in both type definitions and code comments for the writer despite being an unkeyed hash.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The two chain mechanisms were developed independently (audit-writer.ts Sprint 208, audit-export.ts Sprint 211) without a shared algorithm contract — an architectural inconsistency in the audit integrity guarantees.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: Confirmed both cited locations conflict. audit-writer.ts:166-169 computeEventHmac uses `createHash('sha256')` (UNKEYED) over `prevHmac + canonicalJson(basePayload)` (sorted-key deterministic), stored in field `AuditEvent.hmac` (line 44 comment 'sha256(prevHmac + canonicalJson(...))'). audit-export.ts:114-116 buildHmacChain uses `createHmac('sha256', secret)` (KEYED, default secret 'deckent-audit' at line 45/76) over `prev + JSON.stringify(entry)` (insertion-order serialization). Different primitive (createHash vs createHmac), different key (none vs secret), different serialization (canonicalJson vs JSON.stringify) → mutually unverifiable. The writer field is misleadingly named 'hmac' despite being an unkeyed hash. Confirmed. (Minor: original evidence quoted `.join(',')` but actual code is `.digest('hex')` — does not affect the inconsistency claim.)

confirmed.description: The data and extended capability handlers declare requiredCapability strings ('db.read', 'mail.read', 'net.read', 'env.read', 'shell.exec') that are not in the canonical Capability union and are not present in any role's grant set in ROLE_CAPABILITY_MAP. confirmed.suspectedRootCause: F8 handlers were added with new fine-grained capability verbs before the Capability union and ROLE_CAPABILITY_MAP were updated to include them. The type cast suppresses the compile error but the semantic mismatch persists.

confirmed.title: CascadeDetector.onResult does not re-check paused state — sprint can continue processing after PAUSE_SPRINT is returned
confirmed.evidence: cascade-detector.ts:60-96: onResult checks `if (this.halted)` (line 61) and returns early, but does NOT check `if (this.paused)`. After setting `this.paused = true` and returning PAUSE_SPRINT (lines 72-77), a subsequent call to onResult on the same instance (before reset() is called) skips the paused check entirely, increments totalTasks (line 65), and can return CONTINUE, THROTTLE, or PAUSE_SPRINT depending on counters — but never 'you are already paused'. The `paused` field is written (line 72) and read only by getStats() (line 164); it is not a guard in any method except the commented intent. By contrast, the `halted` field IS checked first (line 61).
confirmed.description: The CascadeDetector is documented to pause the sprint on 5 consecutive NO_GO results and require manual resume. However, onResult() does not guard on `this.paused` at its entry point (unlike `this.halted`). If a caller ignores the PAUSE_SPRINT signal and continues calling onResult(), the detector will process further results as if un-paused: it will reset consecutiveNoGo on a non-NO_GO result (line 80), potentially allowing indefinite continuation. This structural asymmetry between the `paused` and `halted` flags means the PAUSE_SPRINT guarantee is advisory at the detector level — and, as noted in the unwired finding above, the detector is not wired to production at all, compounding this structural gap.
confirmed.cluster: core/capability-cluster (auth-session, capability-audit-bridge, capability-broker, capability-handlers-data, capability-handlers, capability-runtime, capability-spec, cascade-detector)
confirmed.verifyEvidence: cascade-detector.ts:60-97 onResult: line 61 guards `if (this.halted) return HALT_SPRINT` but there is NO `if (this.paused)` guard at entry. Line 72 sets `this.paused = true` then returns PAUSE_SPRINT (lines 73-77). A subsequent onResult call skips any paused check, increments totalTasks (line 65), and on a non-NO_GO result resets consecutiveNoGo to 0 (line 80) → can return CONTINUE/THROTTLE indefinitely. `paused` field is read only by getStats() (line 166), never as a method guard. Asymmetry vs `halted` (checked first) confirmed; PAUSE_SPRINT is advisory at detector level.

confirmed.title: like operator has divergent semantics across ERP drivers: SQL wildcards vs. literal substring
confirmed.evidence: In-memory driver (handler.ts line 137-140): `/** Translate an SQL LIKE pattern (\`%\` any-run, \`_\` single char) */` — uses likePatternToRegExp which converts % to .* and _ to .. IFS driver (ifs/driver.ts line 118-120): passes value raw to `contains(field,'${literal}')` — % and _ are OData literal chars. SAP driver (sap/driver.ts line 112-117): passes to `substringof('${literal}', field)` — same, wildcards become literals. Odoo driver (odoo/driver.ts line 62): maps 'like' → 'ilike' which Odoo treats as SQL-style LIKE with % and _ wildcards.
confirmed.description: The four drivers disagree on what 'like' means for the user. In-memory and Odoo honor SQL LIKE wildcards (% = any sequence, _ = any char). IFS and SAP silently discard the wildcard meaning and perform a plain substring search for the literal value including any % or _ characters. A query with filter {field:'name', op:'like', value:'Foo%'} returns rows starting with 'Foo' on in-memory/Odoo but only rows containing the literal string 'Foo%' on IFS/SAP. The connector schema (connector.ts) does not document which semantic is authoritative.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: handler.ts:139-141 likePatternToRegExp converts %→.* and _→. (SQL wildcards). ifs/driver.ts:117-120 `like` → `contains(field,'literal')` (literal substring, % stays literal). sap/driver.ts:112-117 `like` → `substringof('literal', field)` (literal substring). odoo/driver.ts:62 `like: 'ilike'` (Odoo ilike honors SQL %/_ wildcards). In-memory+Odoo honor wildcards; IFS+SAP treat them literally — genuine divergence confirmed across all four cited locations.

confirmed.title: PanicGuard BLOCK decision is advisory-only: the worker kill proceeds regardless
confirmed.evidence: Lines 1213–1245: `const panicGuard = new PanicGuard(projectRoot); const decision = panicGuard.evaluate(..., undefined, ...)`. When `decision === 'BLOCK'` (line 1223) the code logs `debugLog(...)` (line 1224), writes a synthetic NO_GO result (lines 1225–1244), and calls `results.push(syntheticResult)` — but does NOT kill the process. The opts argument is `undefined` (line 1219), so `isAllowed = false` always and `decision` is always `'BLOCK'` in the grace-kill path. The guard then returns BLOCK, and the kill is silently omitted without any user-visible notification. `buildNotification()` is never called, no `notify()` is issued, and the user receives no signal that a kill was blocked.
confirmed.description: The panic guard was designed to block unilateral worker kills and require user approval (Alperen rule). But the implementation does the opposite of blocking: it writes a synthetic NO_GO and continues — the practical effect is the worker is abandoned rather than killed, with no user notification. The guard's ALLOW path (requiring `force && userExplicit`) can never be reached in normal grace-kill flow because opts is always `undefined` at line 1219. The guard logs to debugLog (not visible to the user) and never dispatches a human-checkpoint-required notification. This means: (1) the user never knows a kill was blocked, (2) workers that should have been killed are silently abandoned, and (3) the approval workflow is completely unreachable from this code path.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The panic guard and the approval workflow (cli/commands/nervous.ts:acceptPanicGuard, mcp/tools/nervous.ts) were built in a later sprint than the grace-kill logic. The integration step — wiring `buildNotification` into `notify()` + providing a way to re-trigger the kill on approval — was never implemented. The guard records the event to a JSON file (writePanicLog) but no reader of that file feeds back into the kill decision.

confirmed.title: OutputCollector uses spawnSync for docker/tmux polling, blocking the event loop in the hot polling path

The `followDockerOutput` in the same file correctly uses async spawn (line 485) — but the polling path ignores this pattern. This contradicts the architecture's own internal example.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The polling functions were written with spawnSync for simplicity (fire-and-read pattern). The follow-mode function added later was correctly made async, but the polling path was never retrofitted. No CI test exercises the polling path with a real docker/tmux process, so the event-loop blockage is invisible in the test suite.

confirmed.title: resolveComposition asymmetric conflict logic: unrestricted skills incorrectly block restricted skills

Then line 186 checks `!skill.composableWith.includes(existing.id)` — if the incoming skill's composableWith does not list the existing unrestricted skill's id, this is TRUE → conflict flagged. Result: a restricted skill (composableWith=['security-specialist']) will be blocked from combining with any unrestricted skill (composableWith=[]) whose id is not in its composableWith list, even though the unrestricted skill imposes no restriction. At least 20 built-in skills have non-empty composableWith arrays (.deckent/skills/*/manifest.json).
confirmed.description: The composition conflict resolution is asymmetric. An unrestricted skill (composableWith=[]) can coexist with anything, but a restricted skill (composableWith non-empty) cannot coexist with any unrestricted skill unless it explicitly lists that skill's id in its composableWith. The intent was to block restricted skills from incompatible combinations, but the implementation also blocks them from valid unrestricted companions. This can silently drop valid skill combinations from the selected set.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The inner loop at line 186 should only apply when the existing skill also has restrictions (similar to the guard at line 180). The missing guard `if (existing.composableWith.length > 0 &&` at line 186 makes the check one-sided.

So when an incoming restricted skill (composableWith non-empty) is compared against an already-resolved unrestricted skill (composableWith=[]), line 180 is skipped (false) but line 186 fires TRUE unless the restricted skill explicitly lists the unrestricted skill's id — flagging a conflict and dropping the combination. confirmed.title: RBAC enforcement is permanently soft by default — enforce_rbac flag defaults to false, making the authority check advisory-only with no block path in standard configuration
confirmed.evidence: Lines 351-378: `const enforced = opts.enforceRbac === true; ... if (enforced) { return { allowed: false, level: 'deny', ... }; } console.warn(...); return { allowed: true, level: 'warn', ... };`. The `enforceRbac` flag defaults to `false` everywhere it is passed: backlog-trigger.ts:31 `const enforceRbac = (config as ConfigWithRbac).enforce_rbac === true`, sprint-runtime.ts:30 same pattern. Since `enforce_rbac` is absent from the standard config and defaults false, `checkWorkerAuthority` ALWAYS returns `allowed: true` for role violations — a worker with role 'viewer' requesting 'db-write' gets `level: 'warn'` but `allowed: true`, and its spawn proceeds.
confirmed.description: The ADR-037 RBAC authority matrix is structurally implemented but architecturally non-blocking by design. The gateway function `checkWorkerAuthority` accepts all requests when `enforceRbac` is false (the default), regardless of whether the actor role permits the requested capabilities. Even when callers correctly check `result.allowed`, the value is always `true` in soft mode. The audit-trail and console.warn fire but the operation is never blocked. This means the entire role-based authority control system provides zero enforcement in default deployments — it is a pure auditing mechanism, not an access control mechanism, despite the interface implying otherwise (the `allowed: boolean` return field and the `deny` level suggest blocking behavior).
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The comment at authority-matrix.ts:192-194 explicitly acknowledges this: 'ADR-037 RBAC V1.0 is advisory (allow-all, NO_OP). ENT-1 takes a real V2 step ... Enforcement stays SOFT (warn+emit) by default — backward-safe ... only HARD blocks when the caller passes the opt-in enforce_rbac config flag (default false).' This is a deliberate architectural choice documented as V1.0/pre-GA soft enforcement, but the flag has no default-true path and `enforce_rbac` is not even declared on `ResolvedConfig` (it's a type-cast union `ConfigWithRbac`), making hard enforcement effectively unreachable in production without undocumented manual config surgery.

confirmed.title: Signal C (sequence monotonicity) in isWorkerStale can NEVER suppress a stale alert — logical dead code
confirmed.evidence: In `scanHeartbeats` (line 488): `const hb = readHeartbeatCached(hbPath)`. Inside `readHeartbeatCached` (lines 63–86), whenever mtime has changed the cache entry is written with `lastSequence: hb.sequence ?? 0` (line 78). Control then passes to `isWorkerStale` (line 498). Inside `isWorkerStale` Signal C (lines 410–415): `const cached = heartbeatCache.get(hbPath)` retrieves the entry that was just updated — so `cached.lastSequence` equals `hb.sequence` unconditionally. The guard `(hb.sequence ?? 0) > cached.lastSequence` therefore evaluates to `false` always, and Signal C never fires.
confirmed.description: The three-signal stale-detection strategy documents Signal C as a guard against false-positive stale alerts when a worker is active but heartbeat mtime was unchanged. In practice the guard is structurally tautological: `readHeartbeatCached` must be called before `isWorkerStale` (to get the `hb` object), and that call overwrites `lastSequence` to the current sequence before the comparison is made. The comparison will always be `n > n → false`. Any worker that genuinely increases its sequence between two scan cycles cannot benefit from this suppression; only Signals A and B protect against false positives.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: Signal C was designed for a pattern where the cache entry persists between scan cycles and the lastSequence field preserves the value from the previous read. But `readHeartbeatCached` updates `lastSequence` on EVERY mtime-changing read, so by the time `isWorkerStale` checks it the baseline has already advanced. The fix would be to snapshot `lastSequence` before the re-read and compare against that snapshot, not the post-read cache.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: scanHeartbeats calls readHeartbeatCached(hbPath) at line 488 BEFORE isWorkerStale at line 498. readHeartbeatCached (58-86) on every mtime-changed read writes the cache entry with lastSequence: hb.sequence ?? 0 (line 78). Signal C at 410-414 then does heartbeatCache.get(hbPath) and tests (hb.sequence ?? 0) > cached.lastSequence; since cached.lastSequence was just set to hb.sequence, this is n > n = false unconditionally. Same hb object/sequence flows through both. Tautology confirmed.

confirmed.title: checkWorkerAuthority always returns true — scope violation enforcement is permanently disabled
confirmed.evidence: Lines 600–620: `if (!result.allowed) { console.warn(...); emitAuthorityViolation(...); return true; } return true;` — both branches of the `if (!result.allowed)` block return `true`. The function signature declares `boolean` return but the value carries no information: whether the authority check passes or fails, the caller receives `true`. The ADR-037 comment at line 603 acknowledges this: `[ADR-037 soft]`. This is separate from the `authority-matrix.ts::checkWorkerAuthority` (which has a proper `allowed: false` deny path under `enforceRbac=true`). The worker.ts version is the one directly callable by worker code for file-write scope checks.
confirmed.description: Workers call checkWorkerAuthority() to gate file writes outside their assigned scope. Because both branches unconditionally return true, the function never actually blocks an out-of-scope write — it only logs and emits a telemetry event. Any worker can write any file with no enforcement. The Auditor detects violations post-hoc via git diff --stat, but no real-time blocking occurs at write time. This means the ADR-037 RBAC guarantee is structurally hollow in this code path.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The second `return true` on line 617 (inside the `if (!result.allowed)` block) was intentionally placed as the V1.0 soft-mode design — ADR-037 V1.0 explicitly deferred hard blocking to V2 post-GA. However, the return value is also `true` on the allowed path (line 620), making the boolean return type meaningless. Even if a caller wanted to check the return and block, it cannot distinguish allowed from denied.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: worker.ts:602-620 read directly: `if (!result.allowed) { console.warn('[ADR-037 soft] ...'); if (sprintId) emitAuthorityViolation(...); return true; } return true;` — both the deny branch (line 617) and the allow branch (line 620) unconditionally `return true`. Comment '[ADR-037 soft]' at line 603. Return value carries no allow/deny information; no real-time block.

confirmed.title: trace-recorder.appendTrace() uses synchronous blocking I/O (appendFileSync) on the hot per-turn path, violating ADR-087
confirmed.evidence: trace-recorder.ts:9: `import { appendFileSync, mkdirSync } from 'node:fs';`; trace-recorder.ts:40-42: `export function appendTrace(filePath: string, example: TrainingExample): void { mkdirSync(dirname(filePath), { recursive: true }); appendFileSync(filePath, JSON.stringify(example) + '\n', 'utf-8'); }`. Called from trace-wire.ts:24 and wired into native-agent-bridge.ts:122: `if (deps.recordTurn) deps.recordTurn(session.transcript())` — executed at the end of every completed turn. ADR-087 (Async I/O & Test Hermeticity Standard, accepted, visible in .brain/exports/decisions.md) mandates async I/O and no blocking synchronous calls. mkdirSync + appendFileSync block the Node.js event loop on every turn completion.
confirmed.description: The training-trace recorder uses two synchronous file system calls (mkdirSync + appendFileSync) on the main event loop at the end of each agent turn. This is a structural ADR-087 violation: the blocking I/O stalls all other async work (incoming events, Ink render updates) for the duration of the disk write. On high-load or slow storage, this causes visible REPL stutter. The guard DECKENT_TRACE=0 opt-out exists but is not the default, so all users hit this path unless they explicitly opt out.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: trace-recorder.ts was authored as 'a thin, pure mapping + an fs append' (file header comment) and chose synchronous I/O for simplicity. No async variant or queue was implemented. ADR-087 was either not applied at authoring time or was added after.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: trace-recorder.ts:9 `import { appendFileSync, mkdirSync } from 'node:fs'`; :40-42 appendTrace = mkdirSync(...) + appendFileSync(...). Wired per completed turn: native-agent-bridge.ts:122 `if (deps.recordTurn) deps.recordTurn(session.transcript())` → trace-wire.ts:24 appendTrace(...). Default-on: run.tsx:197 `enabled: process.env['DECKENT_TRACE'] !== '0'` (opt-out only). ADR-087 (accepted, decisions.md:9363+) Rule 2: 'Hot-path file/network I/O async ... A one-shot small config read at startup MAY stay sync.' Per-turn append is on the agent turn path, not the startup-config exception, so it is a real sync-I/O finding. Severity note: it runs once per turn (not in a tight loop/scan cycle like ADR-087's cited spawnSync cases), so practical event-loop stall is bounded — closer to medium/low than the high-frequency hot-path the ADR primarily targets; the structural sync-I/O-on-turn-path claim itself is confirmed.

confirmed.title: `DeriveRequestPrincipalOptions.authGateVerified` / `RequestPrincipal.claimsVerified` never set in production

No production caller ever sets this flag. Every principal returned in production has `claimsVerified` absent (falsy). Any consumer that gates a cross-tenant or role-based decision on `claimsVerified` will always see the unverified-claims path, defeating the intended defense-in-depth.

confirmed.title: output-stream sends duplicate lines when CircularBuffer has dropped entries — slice index arithmetic is wrong under overflow
confirmed.evidence: Lines 211-225: `if (snapshot.totalLinesReceived > sentLineCount) { const allLines = snapshot.lines; const newLinesCount = snapshot.totalLinesReceived - sentLineCount; const newLines = allLines.slice(-newLinesCount); ... }`. `snapshot.lines` = `CircularBuffer.getAll()` = at most `DEFAULT_MAX_LINES` (10 000) entries. `snapshot.totalLinesReceived` = `buffer.received` which counts ALL lines including dropped ones. When `droppedLines > 0`, `totalLinesReceived > lines.length`. If `sentLineCount` is behind enough that `newLinesCount >= allLines.length`, `allLines.slice(-newLinesCount)` returns the ENTIRE buffer (JS semantics: `arr.slice(-n)` where `n >= arr.length` === `arr.slice(0)`). Lines the client already received in the snapshot are re-sent as 'output' events.
confirmed.description: After a buffer overflow event (> 10k lines), the SSE output-stream endpoint resends the entire buffered output to any connected client on the next poll tick, flooding the dashboard with duplicate (already-seen) log lines. This is a silent wrong-result: no error is raised, polling continues, and the client's log view accumulates duplicate entries.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The line-counting logic tracks `totalLinesReceived` (a monotone counter including dropped lines) as the cursor, but indexes into `snapshot.lines` (a capped buffer) using the difference. The two counts diverge as soon as the buffer overflows, and the arithmetic produces an index larger than the buffer, making `slice` return the full array.
confirmed.cluster: api-endpoint-layer (evolution, live-events, memory-search, token-middleware, missions, nervous, oidc-callback, output-stream)
confirmed.verifyEvidence: output-stream.ts:211-225: newLinesCount = snapshot.totalLinesReceived - sentLineCount; newLines = allLines.slice(-newLinesCount). output-collector.ts confirms divergence: getSnapshot (299-309) sets totalLinesReceived = buffer.received (=totalReceived incl. dropped, line 112/96) and lines = buffer.getAll() (capped, line 122; overflow drops oldest at 99-100). So after overflow totalLinesReceived > lines.length. When sentLineCount lags enough that newLinesCount >= allLines.length, JS slice(-n) with n>=length returns the WHOLE array — already-sent lines re-emitted as 'output' events. Arithmetic bug confirmed.

There is no `return` or `socket.destroy()` on the mTLS detection branch.
confirmed.description: When a TLS client presents a certificate during WebSocket upgrade, the gateway detects it, optionally emits a console.warn, and then does nothing — the connection proceeds to standard bearer-token auth as if no cert was presented. This is a no-op gate: the mTLS path is structurally wired to 'warn but never block.' A client cert cannot substitute for or reinforce token auth; it is silently ignored. If the system ever deploys in a configuration where cert presence is expected to be authoritative (sub-project #3), this fall-through allows unauthenticated clients holding a cert to proceed to the token check — and if they also supply the token, they are admitted with an unverified cert identity.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The mTLS seam was added as a future extension point (sub-project #3) with a comment block but no blocking logic. The code path warns but does not call `socket.destroy()` or return early, so cert presence is advisory-only.
confirmed.cluster: api/terminal — PTY gateway, auth providers, guards, outbound limiter
confirmed.verifyEvidence: Verified personally. ws-gateway.ts:51-62: detects `tlsSocket.getPeerCertificate()`, and if `peerCert.raw` present with no `deps.auth.verifyClientCert` it `console.warn`s; the actual verify call is a comment only (line 59). No `return`, no `socket.destroy()` — control flows to token parse at line 64 and proceeds to the standard auth gate (81-114). verifyClientCert is an optional unimplemented seam (auth-provider.ts:34); grep finds no production implementation. Guarantee is advisory-only / warn-but-never-block as claimed.

confirmed.title: formatDoctorResponse always reports all checks as failed — .ok vs .passed field mismatch
confirmed.evidence:
Line 37: `checks?: Array<{ ok: boolean; name?: string; ... }>` — DoctorData interface expects `.ok` on each check.
Line 166: `const passed = checks.filter(c => c.ok).length;`
Line 180: `const failedChecks = checks.filter(c => !c.ok);`

But the actual DoctorResult from `runDoctorChecks()` (src/core/config-types.ts line 996-1004) has `{ name: string; passed: boolean; ... }` — it uses `.passed`, not `.ok`.

In `doctor.ts` line 83: `const summary = formatDoctorResponse(response as DoctorData);` — the cast silences the type error, so real check objects with `.passed` are passed to `formatDoctorResponse`, which reads `.ok`. Since `.ok` is `undefined` on real checks, `filter(c => c.ok)` always returns 0 and `filter(c => !c.ok)` returns ALL checks.

Result: the human-readable summary (`json:false`, the default) always says 'System has N issues' and lists ALL checks as failed, regardless of actual health. The JSON output and healthScore (computed from `.passed` at doctor.ts line 65) are correct; only the summary string is wrong.
confirmed.description: The `formatDoctorResponse` helper in `format.ts` reads `c.ok` from each check entry, but the real `DoctorResult.checks[]` emitted by `runDoctorChecks()` uses `c.passed` instead of `c.ok`. The `doctor.ts` MCP tool casts the result to `DoctorData` at line 83 without field mapping, so in production the summary always signals total failure. The tests in `format.test.ts` use synthetic `{ok: true/false}` data (matching the `DoctorData` interface) and `tools.test.ts` mocks `formatDoctorResponse` entirely — neither test exercises the real end-to-end path and therefore neither catches this bug.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The `DoctorData` interface in `format.ts` was defined independently from `DoctorResult`/`DoctorCheck` in `config-types.ts`/`doctor-checks.ts`, causing an `.ok` vs `.passed` naming divergence. The `as DoctorData` cast at `doctor.ts:83` suppresses the TypeScript error that would have flagged this.

confirmed.title: Writer-lease heartbeat is only refreshed on write calls — idle owner window loses lease after 2 minutes

There is no background `setInterval` anywhere in src/mcp/ to refresh the heartbeat, confirmed by grep across all src/mcp/*.ts files returning no setInterval results.
confirmed.description: The MCP writer-lease heartbeat is refreshed exclusively on write tool calls. An owner window that is open but has made no write tool call for 120 seconds will have its lease stolen by the next window that makes a write call, even though the owning process is still alive. A user doing read-only operations (status checks, memory queries) for more than 2 minutes will silently lose write access to their session without any notification. The lease.ok comment at line 9 acknowledges this is advisory, but the silent mid-session ownership transfer creates an unexpected experience.

confirmed.title: AuditChainRow.id typed as number but MemoryStore.queryAuditChain returns id as string; type-safety bypassed with never[] cast
confirmed.evidence:
Line 38: `const result = verifyAuditChain({ store: store as unknown as { queryAuditChain: () => never[] }, secret });`

In `audit-integrity.ts:32-38`, `AuditChainRow.id` is typed `number`. In `memory-store.ts:1083-1103`, `queryAuditChain()` returns `Array<{ id: string; ... }>`. At runtime verifyAuditChain receives a real MemoryStore, calls `queryAuditChain()` correctly, but populates `firstTamperedRowId` (typed `number | null` per `VerifyAuditChainResult`) with an actual `string` value. The display at audit-verify.ts:45 still works via string interpolation, but JSON consumers of `--json` output receive a `string` where the schema declares `number`.
confirmed.description: Two divergent definitions of the audit chain row's `id` field (string in MemoryStore, number in AuditChainStore) are papered over by a `never[]` cast that discards TypeScript's type check entirely. The correct fix is to align `AuditChainRow.id` with the actual DB representation (`string`) and update `VerifyAuditChainResult.firstTamperedRowId` accordingly.

confirmed.title: `deckent nervous edit` bypasses the live-executor IPC gate, causing two-writer race and audit divergence
confirmed.evidence: Lines 323–334: `handleAccept` checks `isNervousPollerAlive(root)` and routes to `NervousIpcQueue.writeApproval()` when the executor is live, explicitly refusing to mutate `pending`/`history` directly. Lines 354–372: `handleReject` does the same. Lines 376–400: `handleEdit` does NOT call `isNervousPollerAlive` at all — it always calls `appendHistoryRecord` and `writePendingNotifications` directly (lines 392–395), regardless of whether a live executor owns those files. Comment on lines 329–334 explicitly states: 'The CLI must NOT mutate pending/history here' when executor is live.
confirmed.description: When the Nervous System executor process is running, `accept` and `reject` correctly route through the IPC queue so the executor's parked approval promise resolves, and only the executor writes the result. `edit`, however, directly mutates both the pending queue and the history file, creating a two-writer race: the executor may concurrently be reading/writing the same files. This can cause history records to be lost or doubled, pending entries to be removed without the executor noticing (leaving parked promises hanging forever), and audit-trail divergence between what the executor recorded and what the CLI wrote.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The APPROVE-007 IPC gate was retrofitted onto `accept`/`reject` (Sprint 280) but `handleEdit` was not updated. The code comment in `handleAccept` (line 329) explicitly warns of the single-writer constraint but `handleEdit` has no equivalent guard.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: Read nervous.ts: handleAccept (lines 323-327) gates on `if (isNervousPollerAlive(root))` → NervousIpcQueue.writeApproval, with comment 329-334 'CLI must NOT mutate pending/history'. handleReject (lines 354-358) same gate. handleEdit (lines 376-400) contains NO isNervousPollerAlive call (grep of 404-435/376-400 region confirms absent) and always runs appendHistoryRecord(392) + writePendingNotifications(395) directly regardless of live executor.

confirmed.title: filterByDateRange silently returns all data for any real calendar date — broken date-to-sprint-number encoding
confirmed.evidence: analytics-data.ts lines 156-164: `function extractSprintNumber(date: Date): number | null { if (date.getFullYear() <= 1970) { const ms = date.getTime(); if (ms >= 0 && ms < 10000) return ms; } return null; }` — returns null for any date after 1970. confirmed.verifyEvidence: analytics-data.ts:156-165 extractSprintNumber returns null unless date.getFullYear()<=1970 AND ms<10000 — null for any post-1970 calendar date. Lines 123-126 fallback `if (fromNum===null||toNum===null) return data;` returns ALL data. The real SharedMemory store (`src/orchestra/shared-memory.ts`) tracks keys written by workers to `.tasks/shared/{key}.json`, and the server never exposes this count via any API endpoint that the dashboard could read. The displayed count therefore misleads operators who expect to see inter-worker data handoff volume.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The Sprint 279 COMM-1 implementation plan described a 'shared-context key count' widget, but the actual implementation used doneAgents.length as a proxy because the backend API to query SharedMemory keys was not built. The misleading JSDoc was never corrected.

confirmed.title: WorkersPage kill failure is silently swallowed with no user feedback — operator blindness on kill failure
confirmed.evidence: Lines 143-154: `const handleKill = useCallback(async (agentId: string) => { if (!confirm(...)) return; try { await postJson('/api/kill/' + agentId); refresh(); } catch { // error handled silently — next poll/SSE tick reconciles the grid } }, [refresh, t]);`. The catch block is empty with a comment stating the SSE tick will reconcile — but if the kill POST fails (e.g., network error, 403, 500), the worker is NOT killed, and the operator receives no feedback. There is no error state variable set in the catch, no toast/alert rendered, and no visual indicator that the kill command failed.
confirmed.description: When an operator clicks 'Kill Worker' and the API call fails, the UI silently continues with no error message. The premise 'next poll/SSE tick reconciles the grid' is wrong for a kill failure: the grid reconciling will show the worker still alive, but the operator has no indication the kill was rejected vs. the worker being re-spawned. This is an advisory-only pattern where a user-initiated destructive action fails without notifying the user, which is especially dangerous for sprint management: an operator might believe a worker was killed when it is still consuming resources and writing results.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: The structural root cause is a missing error-state variable in handleKill. Other action handlers in the codebase (e.g., NervousPage.tsx handleAccept/handleReject at lines 72-98) correctly capture errors with `setActionError()` and render them to the user. WorkersPage adopted the same pattern for the confirm dialog but omitted the error-state machinery for the kill POST failure path.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: WorkersPage.tsx (read) handleKill lines 143-154: `try { await postJson('/api/kill/'+agentId); refresh(); } catch { // error handled silently — next poll/SSE tick reconciles the grid }` — empty catch, no error-state variable, no toast/alert. Contrast NervousPage.tsx lines 69/79-80/93-94: declares `setActionError` state and `catch (err) { setActionError(err...) }` rendering the error to the user. WorkersPage genuinely omits the error-state machinery present elsewhere; the guarantee (user feedback on destructive-action failure) is not enforced.

confirmed.title: aligned and general corpora share the same MsgExample object references
confirmed.description: Both `general` and `aligned` receive the exact same object reference. Any downstream consumer (e.g. in scripts/extract-traces.mjs) that mutates a `general` entry — such as adding/removing messages, or transforming tool_calls — will silently mutate the corresponding `aligned` entry too. The two corpora are semantically distinct (aligned = core-4-only remapped; general = all tools), but the shared reference erases that boundary the moment either array is post-processed or serialized with mutation. No defensive copy (`{ ...example }` or `structuredClone`) is made before the conditional push to `aligned`.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: Missing defensive copy on the conditional `aligned` push. The author assumed the two arrays would only be read and serialized, not mutated — a fragile assumption that is not structurally enforced and will silently corrupt the aligned corpus if the pipeline evolves.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: Read cc-trace-extractor.ts lines 57-63: flush() builds `const example: MsgExample = {...}` once, then `general.push(example)` (line 60) and `if (!current.hasNonMappable) aligned.push(example)` (line 61) — the SAME object reference pushed to both arrays, no `{...example}`/structuredClone. Consumer scripts/extract-traces.mjs (line 42-43) only does `aligned.push(...r.aligned)` and JSON.stringify serialization (read-only, no mutation today), so this is a real latent fragility exactly as described: corpus-distinctness is structurally unenforced and any future mutation of a general entry would corrupt the shared aligned entry. Confirmed.

confirmed.title: tool_result tool_call_id silently falls back to empty string, producing invalid OpenAI messages
confirmed.description: The OpenAI messages format requires `tool_call_id` to be a non-empty string that matches the `id` of the preceding `tool_calls` entry. When a CC transcript `tool_result` block is missing `tool_use_id` (malformed or partial session), the extractor silently emits `tool_call_id: ''`. This produces structurally invalid training examples that will be accepted into both `general` and `aligned` corpora without any warning or skip — causing silent training data corruption. The same pattern on the assistant side (line 141: `id: (b['id'] as string) ?? ''`) has the symmetric problem for tool_calls.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: Defensive nullish coalescing was applied uniformly to all string fields without distinguishing required-non-empty fields from optional ones. No validation or skip guard exists for the case where the id fields are absent.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: Read cc-trace-extractor.ts lines 107-111: `tool_call_id: (b['tool_use_id'] as string) ?? ''` with no skip/validation guard; symmetric line 141: `id: (b['id'] as string) ?? ''`. When the id field is absent the extractor emits an empty string and the message is still pushed into current.messages and later accepted into both corpora (general line 60, aligned line 61) with no skip. No validation guard exists anywhere in the function for empty ids. The defect described (silent invalid training examples) is structurally present. Note: the two cited lines are parallel instances of the same gap, not a self-conflict, but the underlying defect is real and confirmed in code.

confirmed.title: CORE4 map is private and unreachable by any external caller needing to enumerate mappable tool names
confirmed.description: The `CORE4` constant encodes the complete mapping of CC core-4 tool names to deckent natives, but it is module-private (not exported). `mapToolName` exposes only point-lookup (one name at a time). Any pipeline logic that needs to enumerate or validate the full set of mappable names (e.g. to report which tools were remapped vs kept) must either re-implement the list or call `mapToolName` speculatively. This is a low-severity API design gap — not a runtime bug, but it means `scripts/extract-traces.mjs` cannot produce a summary of which tool names were remapped without duplicating the CORE4 list. Confirmed by grep: no production caller reads `CORE4` directly; the constant is only referenced within `mapToolName` at line 21.
confirmed.suspectedRootCause: CORE4 was written as an implementation detail of `mapToolName` with no anticipation that callers would need enumeration. Adding `export const DECKENT_TOOL_NAMES = Object.values(CORE4)` would close the gap.
confirmed.verifyEvidence: grep -rn 'CORE4' across src/ and scripts/ (excluding tests and def file) returns NO hits; within cc-trace-extractor.ts CORE4 is declared at lines 12-17 (no `export`) and referenced only at line 21 inside `mapToolName`. The sole external consumer scripts/extract-traces.mjs (line 24) imports only `extractFromSession`, never CORE4 nor any enumeration export. So the full mappable-name set is module-private and only point-lookup (mapToolName) is exposed — an enumeration caller would have to re-implement the list. Low-severity API-design gap confirmed.
